text.front:
Tyrant and Penitent: Nebuchadnezzar and Biblical
Exemplarity
Jake Wiseman
Department of English Language and Literature, University College London, London, UK
ABSTRACT
At the end of the fourth chapter of the Book of Daniel, the
Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar is punished for his pride. He is
cast out from his kingdom, forced to eat grass with wild beasts,
and repents before being restored to his throne. This article
examines the encounters between this ancient biblical narrative,
humanist rhetoric of exemplarity, and reformed doctrines of
repentance. Nebuchadnezzar's narrative tested the capacity of
exemplarity to absorb singular biblical texts into reformed
theologies. Exemplarity offered John Calvin a rhetorical tool with
which to refashion Nebuchadnezzar as a model of reformed
penitential doctrine. The article shows that the popular preacher
Henry Smith (c. 1560-91) read Calvin's lectures on Daniel, and
applied Nebuchadnezzar's example to the lives of his Elizabethan
congregants. Annotations and a manuscript notebook reveal that
readers turned to Smith's sermons for the extractable moral and
spiritual lessons carried by Nebuchadnezzar's exemplary narrative.
KEYWORDS
Nebuchadnezzar; Book of
Daniel; Bible; Henry Smith;
Calvin; exemplarity

text.body:
the historian Thomas Fuller (1608-61), the church was often so full that "Persons of good
quality" were forced to stand in the aisles to hear the so-called "silver-tongued" preacher. 3
Addressing this packed congregation, Smith delivered a triad of sermons on Nebuchad-
nezzar's pride, fall, and restitution. The texts of these sermons were taken from the fourth
chapter of the biblical Book of Daniel, which narrates Nebuchadnezzar's punishment for
his pride and subsequent repentance. The king is exiled from his kingdom to eat grass
among wild beasts, growing his hair "like egles feathers" and his nails "like birds
clawes" until he repents (Dan. 4:30). 4 In his sermons, Smith held up the Babylonian
king as an example for his congregants, announcing, "Heere is a glasse for all the children
of pride," urging them to "looke upon Nebuchadnezzar, you which are great men like
Nebuchadnezzar. For thus will God make his examples of great men, because they
should be examples to others" (Sermons, N4 v ). Nebuchadnezzar offered a vivid image
for Smith's congregants to "looke upon" as both a warning against pride and an exhor-
tation towards repentance. In this rhetorical and homiletic maneuver, Smith initiated a
chain of exemplarity where an outward display of repentance was vital in order to inspire
others to do the same. Smith moves fluently between the twin impulses of the exemplary
narrative: a memorable story on the one hand, and universal application on the other.
However, the narrative of Nebuchadnezzar's fall in Daniel 4 was not easy to assimilate
into the universalizing rhetoric of exemplarity. The image of the fallen king eating grass
was highly memorable, but it was also remote, arcane, and accompanied by a long tradi-
tion of reading Nebuchadnezzar's punishment to prefigure the sacrament of penance.
Here, Smith deployed another element of his "silver-tongued" skill: his ability to repack-
age reformed theology for a popular English audience. In this case, he turned to John
Calvin's lectures on Daniel 4, which used exemplarity as both a rhetorical and doctrinal
tool. Calvin fashioned Nebuchadnezzar as a "notorious example for all ages," insisting
that "thys punishment which God hath layd upon the king of Babylon is an example
for us." 5 Calvin proposed a rhetorical solution to the problems that arose when reformed
doctrine collided with the narrative details of scripture. A rhetoric of exemplarity offered
the means to turn Nebuchadnezzar's actions into an external proof of interior repen-
tance. Consequently, Calvin turned Nebuchadnezzar into a paradigmatic instance of
reformed penitential doctrine. This, in turn, animated Smith's sermons, where the
preacher cast this ancient narrative of exile and debasement as a timely warning for
his Elizabethan congregation. Tracing Nebuchadnezzar from Calvin's lectures to the Eliz-
abethan pulpit and, ultimately, a seventeenth-century notebook gives witness to the col-
lision between the singularity of biblical narrative, the opportunities of humanist

and doctrine was capable of reimagining even this most conspicuous scriptural narrative
of a herbivorous and bestial king.
Nebuchadnezzar, for example
By the end of the sixteenth century, Nebuchadnezzar's narrative met with a humanist
culture that was increasingly attenuated to exemplary rhetoric. For humanist authors,
the example was a versatile instrument. It could be positive or negative, used to encour-
age or castigate. 6 As a mode of instruction, it was particularly favored by schoolmasters as
it navigated between maxim and experience. 7 As a rhetorical tool, exemplarity was a
means by which a small narrative unit or image could stand for a larger universal
truth. In early modern England, this relied on the Greek figure of παραδειγμα (parad-
eigma) as a model, translated into Latin as exemplar. 8 Post-Reformation biblical exem-
plarity operated primarily according to a Platonic conception of the example where
units of scriptural narrative pointed towards transcendental religious truths, offering
themselves as models for imitation. 9 According to Henry Peacham's 1577 edition of
The Garden of Eloquence, an example "is the rehearsal of a deede, or saying past, and
applying of it to our purpose." 10 Rhetorical persuasion was central: examples had
"great force to move, perswade, and enfame men with the love of vertue, and also
most mightie to deterre and disswade them from vice." 11 Examples could be drawn
from all genres of historical texts, including the Bible, since "the holye Scriptures have
examples of all sorts." 12 Exemplarity, then, can be distinguished from typology
because it does not specifically anticipate the New Testament or the Christian
Church. 13 Rather, examples served as models of religious ideals, ready for rhetorical or
persuasive use.
However, biblical narrative was not always as pliable as religious authors desired or
exemplarity necessitated. If, as Alexander Gelley has suggested, "[t]he tactic of exemplar-
ity would seem to be to mingle the singular with the normative, to mark an instance as
fated," then biblical narrative was not always able to shirk its singularity. 14 For Nebu-
chadnezzar, a story that was used as an exemplar for redemptive grace could not

text.body:
evade the remote spectacle of a fallen king eating grass. In the revised and expanded 1593
edition of the Garden of Eloquence, Peacham defined the example in terms of its readerly
reception: "These [examples] are they whom wee diligently looke uppon with the eies of
our mindes, and also deepely considering both what they were, what they did, what they
received, and what they suffered." 15 By reading examples in this way, Peacham suggested
that "it plainly appeareth, that there is a most just justice in God." 16 For Peacham, it was
not sufficient only to "looke uppon" examples, but it was also necessary to subject them to
deep consideration to reveal their providential truths. As Timothy Hampton has shown,
early modern examples were subject to a process wherein "a contingent past activity is
raised to a momentary universality that makes discernible its value for the present." 17
In order to render Nebuchadnezzar as a universal Christian example, authors reduced
the contingencies of his narrative. For instance, the narrative in Daniel 4 featured in
Thomas Paynell's 1561 translation of Nicholas de Hannape's The Ensamples of Vertue
and Vice, Gathered Oute of Holye Scripture. The volume, as its title suggests, is full of
exemplary narratives plucked from the Bible. In order to render Nebuchadnezzar as a
universalized example, the work paraphrases his narrative while reducing the particular-
ities of his punishment, stating only that he "was cast oute of mennes companye." 18
Losing the bird claws and eagle feathers allowed the king to feature as an exemplary
model under the heading, "Of humilitie." 19 Details of Nebuchadnezzar's punishment
were more likely to be found in the popular Elizabethan judgement books, given their
interest in the miraculous and the supernatural. 20 Stephen Batman's translation The
Doome Warning All Men to the Judgemente detailed how Nebuchadnezzar's "haires
became rough, and covered his flesh, his nayles grewe like the clawes of byrdes." 21 The
volume even provided a woodcut of Nebuchadnezzar among the beasts (Figure 1). In
the woodcut, Nebuchadnezzar stoops, naked and almost furry, with rabbits in the fore-
ground and goats in the background. The king's stance echoes that of these animals,
crawling on all fours with his head bowed to eat grass. Between morality tales and super-
natural wonders narratives, Nebuchadnezzar's punishment exhibits the tension between
the universal aspirations of the example's moral lesson and the particular details of its
narrative.
Within this framework, Nebuchadnezzar was a particularly useful exemplary figure:
either positive or negative, from both history and scripture. Crucially, he was accompa-
nied by a biblical narrative that was capable of exciting the imagination. Nebuchadnezzar
features in the Bible as a tyrannical ruler, invading conqueror, resolute idolator, and
occasional penitent. He appears in 2 Kings, Ezekiel, Jeremiah and Judith as the king
responsible for the sacking of Jerusalem, but his character comes into sharpest relief in
the Book of Daniel. 22 In the first chapter, Nebuchadnezzar, having conquered Jerusalem,

text.body:
takes captive a group of young Judeans including Daniel, as well as Shadrach, Meshach,
and Abednego. By the second chapter, Nebuchadnezzar has dreamt of a statue in four
parts, composed of four different metals. Daniel interprets this as representing four suc-
cessive kingdoms and the eventual destruction of Babylon. In Daniel 3, Nebuchadnezzar
throws Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego into the fiery furnace and marvels at their
miraculous survival. Yet, in the account of his madness in Daniel 4, Nebuchadnezzar's
character comes into greatest focus. At the outset of the chapter, Nebuchadnezzar
dreams of a tall tree that is felled and its fruit scattered, which Daniel interprets to rep-
resent the king's fall: that he will live for seven years with "the beasts of the fielde: they
shall make thee to eate grasse as the oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dewe of
heaven" (Dan. 4:22). Nebuchadnezzar ignores Daniel's warning, and continues to brag
about his accomplishments. Twelve months later, while the king is admiring his city's
architectural splendor, Daniel's interpretation becomes reality. Nebuchadnezzar is cast
out from his kingdom, forced to eat grass, and grows his nails into bird-like claws. Ulti-
mately, however, he repents to "extoll and magnifie the King of heaven," and is restored
to his kingdom (Dan. 4:34). By Daniel 5, Nebuchadnezzar's son, Belshazzar, has assumed
the throne, and Babylon has returned to idolatry. While the book draws on the conven-
tional biblical narrative of a pagan king humbled before God, John J. Collins has argued
that "[w]hat is noteworthy in Daniel 4, however, is the eventual restoration of the king." 23
The extremity of Nebuchadnezzar's narrative arc is extraordinary, even within the bib-
lical canon.
From the narrative's earliest reception, Nebuchadnezzar was closely associated with
penitential exemplarity. Patristic and medieval authors alike had focused on Nebuchad-
nezzar's experience of suffering as a cautionary example of pride and as a template for
repentance. 24 For Tertullian, writing in the early third century CE, Daniel 4 contained a
seminal instance of exomologesis. 25 According to Tertullian's Treatise on Penitence, Neb-
uchadnezzar enacted a "sacrifice of penance, performing his exomologesis for seven squalid
years, his nails growing wild like the talons of an eagle, his hair unkempt like the shaggy
mane of a lion." 26 The Latin marginalia to John Gower's fourteenth-century Confessio
Amantis regard this narrative as "an instructive example against the vice of empty (or
vain) glory" where the king's punishment involved him "making penance for seven
years." 27 During the sixteenth century, Catholic writers maintained that Nebuchadnezzar's
narrative demonstrated the efficacy of penitential works. In his 1587 commentary on
Daniel, the Spanish Jesuit exegete Benito Pereira noted that Nebuchadnezzar's narrative
demonstrates that "sin can be satisfied through works, fasting, prayer, and charity." 28 In
these texts, Nebuchadnezzar takes on a straightforward exemplary function by simultane-
ously showing and enacting repentance. However, this posed a problem to reformed

text.body:
writers, who were keen to assert that, as Calvin wrote in his Institutes of Christian Religion,
repentance primarily concerned "inward renewal of the mind, which bears with it true cor-
rection of life." 29 Consequently, for Calvin, external works became only "the signs of repen-
tance." 30 Works such as fasting, charity, or confession were helpful "exercises," but they did
not enact repentance themselves. 31 Calvin's language of signaling and showing repentance
merged with a rhetoric of exemplarity to produce a reading of biblical narrative in
which Nebuchadnezzar's punishment shifted away from an expression of outward peniten-
tial processes, and towards an exemplary sign of interiority. However, this shift created
more space between the singularities of Nebuchadnezzar's narrative and the universal
virtue that the narrative embodied. Interior repentance was difficult to figure in a narrative
that was so richly visual, and which described a feathery and exilic punishment. Calvin
worked to bridge this gap through an innovative reading of the narrative, which Smith
would later refit for his Elizabethan congregation.
Pride and penitence
John Calvin lectured on the Book of Daniel to the Genevan Academy between April 1559
and June 1560. A year later, the lectures were transcribed and published in Latin, which
Anthony Gilby translated into English in 1570. 32 When Smith preached on
Nebuchadnezzar, his sermons traced a number of the key themes that Calvin had
expounded in Daniel 4, especially the reformed attitudes towards Nebuchadnezzar and
repentance. Yet Calvin's particular influence is most perceptible in small moments of
extra-biblical detail. Commenting on Daniel 4:26 where Nebuchadnezzar "walked in
the royall palace at Babel," he noted: "Some thinke that Nebuchadnezzar walked upon
the roofe of his palace, from whence hee might see all parts of the citie round about
him" (Dan. 4:26; Sermons, L5 r ). The king's roof walk has no basis in English Bible trans-
lations or commentaries. Even Andrew Willet's exhaustive Hexapla in Danielem makes
no mention of it. 33 However, it does appear in Calvin's Latin lectures, where the reformer
offers a mise-en-scene based on his reading of an Aramaic participle: " ‫מ‬
‫ה‬

(mehallech)
some think that he [Nebuchadnezzar] walked on the roof of his palace, where he was
able to view all parts of the city." 34 Calvin's setting invited an equivalence between the
king's architectural and behavioral haughtiness. This provided ideal material for Smith
to add a sense of place to his unfolding biblical drama. He even lifted Calvin's phrasing
"quidam existimant" into his postulation "Some thinke that." This passage is particularly
instructive because Gilby did not include it in his English translation. Therefore, it is pos-
sible to say with some certainty that Smith was using Calvin's lectures in Latin as the basis
for his own vision of Nebuchadnezzar.

text.body:
Calvin's work on Daniel had established the reformed basis for Nebuchadnezzar's
exemplarity as a cautionary tale against pride and model of repentance. Commenting
upon the final verse of Daniel 4, Calvin extended Nebuchadnezzar's first-person
account of his restitution and gave a prosopopoeia in the voice of the Babylonian
king: "God would set me forth as a notable example, whereby all might know that the
proud are humbled by his hand. For I was puffed up with pride: but God hath thus cor-
rected me by an horrible punishment, that now my example might profit all men" (Com-
mentaries, U3 r ). Using Nebuchadnezzar's voice to channel divine authority, Calvin
considered exemplarity an integral part of the biblical narrative. Smith also offered an
imaginative account of the divine authority behind Nebuchadnezzar's exemplarity. In
his sermon on the king's fall, Smith described Nebuchadnezzar's sepulchre upon
which he envisages the engraving: "Be thou an example to Kings and Rulers, for all
the children of pride, to beware how they set themselves against him who advanced
them" (Sermons, M7 v ). Smith wielded God's epitaphic chisel to set exemplarity as the
primary function of Nebuchadnezzar's narrative.
Smith expanded upon Calvin's lectures to attenuate Nebuchadnezzar to his Elizabe-
than congregants. This was, in part, a homiletic necessity, shifting the genre of
Calvin's theological lectures into a popular sermon. However, it also reflects Smith's
adept use of exemplary rhetoric by juggling both the memorable singularity of Nebu-
chadnezzar's punishment and its applicability to the lives of early modern Londoners.
Calvin had commented on the irony that although Nebuchadnezzar boasted about his
palaces, he was not even the Babylonian ruler responsible for building them: "For all
the Historiographers do agree in this, that that citie was built of Semiramis" (Commen-
taries, S2 v -S3 r ). The lecture refers to the legendary Assyrian Queen Semiramis, who was
credited with rebuilding Babylon by the first-century BCE Greek historian Diodorus
Siculus. 35 Smith also alludes to Semiramis, but Calvin was his direct source. Again, he
lifted passages, phrases, and arguments into his sermon wholesale during an entire
passage on Nebuchadnezzar's architectural boasts (see Table 1). 36 Smith begins by
making the same point as Calvin that "all histories accord, that it was built by Semiramis
before Nebuchadnezzar was borne" (Sermons, L7 r ). Why would the Babylonian king
make such a claim? For Calvin, "the aunswere is easie"; for Smith too, "the answer is
easie" (Commentaries, S3 r ; Sermons, L7 r ). But here, the two begin to diverge. Calvin
used this opportunity to discuss the trappings of kingship: "we know how earthly
kynges do study by all meanes possible to throw downe the glory of others" (Commen-
taries, S3 r ). Set against the nascent French Wars of Religion, Calvin's account is deeply
sceptical of overreaching monarchical authority. 37 As a result, the biblical text exhibits

"a tyannicall kynde of speech, which the tyrauntes do often usurpe" (Commentaries, S3 r ).
For the Genevan reformer, Nebuchadnezzar's words are a tyranny in miniature -a type
of verbal usurpation. The king's architectural brags represent an excessive pride that
Calvin regarded as a hallmark of tyrannical power. Smith, by contrast, stretched the bib-
lical narrative to recast Nebuchadnezzar as an exemplar accessible to his Elizabethan con-
gregation. Smith's sermons refer to neither "tyrants" nor "tyranny." Rather, they
underscore the universality of Nebuchadnezzar's narrative. He does not describe the
pride of "earthly kynges," but uses Nebuchadnezzar for his exemplarity wherein "every
one doth labour to obscure the fame of others" (Commentaries, S3 r ; Sermons, L7 r ). So
too, the corridors power are not palaces or cities but "Schooles, or Hospitals, or Col-
ledges" (Sermons, L7 r ). He proceeds to criticize the English aristocracy directly, noting
that "stately houses and places in England, bare their names of those Lords or others
that doe possesse or owe [sic] them, for the like vanitie" (Sermons, L7 r ). These references
exhorted Smith's noble audience directly using the terms and imagery familiar to six-
teenth-century Londoners.
Smith's Nebuchadnezzar is constantly shifting roles to accommodate the full range of
his audience. In the conclusion to his sermon on Nebuchadnezzar's pride, Smith
exhorted his congregants directly: "let this be in stead of Daniels warning" (Sermons,
M1 v ). In this moment of reversal, the preacher retains in his role as prophet but casts
his audience as a multitude of Nebuchadnezzars. This audacious homiletic strategy is
markedly different from Calvin's emphasis on the qualities of kingship. In the sermon
on Nebuchadnezzar's fall, Smith composed a list of other historical tyrants, who
served as instances of God's ultimate kingship: "How did Antiochus, and Julian, and
Herod, and Saul, and Athalia, and Jezebel, and Richard the third goe from their
throues [sic], as if God had pulled them out by the eares?" (Sermons, M7 r ). This list is
a startling romp through biblical, classical, and Plantagenet history. Smith does not
unite these figures according to their tyrannical policies, but as a series of male and

Yet before I go any further, wee must see wherefore he
sayth that Babylon was builte of him. For all the
Historiographers do agree in this, that that citie was built
of Semiramis. Now, a great whyle after Nebuchadnezer
doth declare it for hys prayse and glory, that he hath
built that citie. But the aunswere is easie. For we know
how earthly kynges do study by all meanes possible to
throw downe the glory of others, that onely they myght
excell and get to them selves a perpetuall name:
especially where they chaunge some thyng in
buildinges, or in palacies, or in Cityes they would seeme
to be the first builders, and so blot them out of memory
of whom the foundations were layd. So it may be that
Babylon was beautified of the king Nebuchadnezer:
therefore doth he translate all the glory unto himselfe,
whereas the greater part should have bene ascribed to
Semiramis and Ninus. Wherefore it is a tyrannicall kynde
of speach, that is, which the tyrauntes do often usurpe,
and commonly whiles they draw to them selves other
mens praises: Therefore (sayth he) I have built it wyth the
strength of my power.
What a vaunt was this to say,that he built Babylon, when all
histories accord, that it was built by Semiramis before
Nebuchadnezzar was borne? therefore why doth he
boast of that which another did?
The answere is easie, why doe other men so now? we see
that every one doth labour to obscure the fame of others,
that they may shine alone, and beare the name
themselves, especially in great buildings: for if they do
but adde or alter any thing in Schooles, or Hospitals, or
Colledges, they looke straight to be counted the founders
of them, and so the founders of many places are
forgotten. So it is like that Nebuchadnezzar did adde or
alter some thing in this cittie, and therfore he took al to
himself, as the fashion hath been ever since. But if none
had built it, but he had been the founder of it (as some
would seeme) yet this had been a proud and arrogant
speech to say, which I have built by the might of my
power: for it was not he which could build Babel, no more
then Nemrod could finish Babel; but unlesse the Lord
build the house, the builders build in vaine. Therefore
when he said by the might of my power, he should have
said, by the might of Gods power.

female rulers struck down by God like troublesome children. They are a representation of
both pride and vainglory by attributing absolute authority to themselves above God.
Casting them as foolish children memorably exposes their sinfulness. The preacher
then goes further still to deny their status, noting that God "had no respect unto their
persons, but used them like beasts" (Sermons, M7 r ). For the purpose of Smith's
sermons, the status of kingship is less significant than the preacher's ability to recast
tyrants as moral exemplars of divine judgement.
Feeling and showing repentance
In order for the Babylonian king to operate as an accessible exemplar against pride, Smith
and Calvin sought to reduce the singularity at the crux of his narrative. Although they
diverged on the nature of Nebuchadnezzar's kingship, Smith and Calvin were in total
accordance on one point: Nebuchadnezzar did not physically transform into a beast. 38
The biblical account stated that he "did eat grasse as the oxen, and his bodie was wet
with the dewe of heaven, til his heeres were growen as egles feathers and his nailes
like birds clawes" (Dan. 4:30). In its similes the biblical account opened up a number
of interpretive possibilities, shifting between the literal description of beastly transforma-
tion and figurative senses of mental, social, or political punishment. There was a tradi-
tion, inherited from patristic and medieval sources, that Nebuchadnezzar underwent a
physical transformation. In Gower's Confessio Amantis, for example, Genius uses Nebu-
chadnezzar as an exemplar against pride. The poem imagines Nebuchadnezzar's emo-
tional reaction to his physical transformation: "When he behield his cote of heres, /
He wept and with ful woful teres." 39 In Gower's text, Nebuchadnezzar experiences
redemptive suffering through his punishment. Reformed texts tended to resist this
reading, arguing that Nebuchadnezzar underwent an internal transformation, but did
not change shape. The notes to the 1560 Geneva Bible made the point most clearly:
"Not that his shape or forme was changed into a beast, but that he was ether striken
mad, and so avoided mans companie, or was cast out for his tyrannie and so wandered
among the beasts, and ate herbes and grasse." 40 This note reflects a belief that there was
nothing supernatural about Nebuchadnezzar's exile. This paved the way for his exem-
plarity, because, as Henry Peacham noted in the 1593 Garden of Eloquence, a good
example should convey "the true and lively Image of time past." 41 In pursuit of this
type of truthful exemplarity, Smith and Calvin reduced the remoteness of Nebuchadnez-
zar's narrative, insisting that it did not involve supernatural transformation. However,
they are less certain about the exact nature of Nebuchadnezzar's non-physical punish-
ment. Reformers were able to fill this hermeneutic gap with doctrines of repentance,
enabling Nebuchadnezzar to act as an exemplary penitent.
Calvin lectured that Nebuchadnezzar's punishment did not involve any physical
"metamorphosis," but "he was so cast forth of mans company, that except onely mans

shape, he differed nothing from brute beastes" (Commentaries, S4 r ). 42 This distinction
was crucial for Calvin to develop his theology into his reading of Nebuchadnezzar's
fall. Yet, for Smith, this becomes a moment of confessional contrast with Catholics
and generic contrast with literary writers:
Now if any man long to be resolved, how this King was changed to a beast, he must not
imagine any strange metamorphosis, or popish transubstantiation, as though his shape
were altred, or his manhood removed, or that he put on hornes and hoofes, as the Poets
faine of Acteon; for the voice doth not say that he should become a beast; but that he
should dwell with the beasts (Sermons, M7 r ).
Smith seized upon Calvin's "metamorphosis" and turned it into an attack on the poets -
in particular Ovid's Metamorphoses -as well as an opportunity to take a swipe at Catholic
eucharistic theology. It is a playful passage, but it also represents an important facet of
Smith's use of Nebuchadnezzar. By insisting that there was no metamorphosis involved
in Nebuchadnezzar's punishment, Smith was able to reinforce its universal exemplarity.
He argued that Nebuchadnezzar's punishment was not a poetic fabulation, but an event
in biblical history capable of conveying religious meaning. Therefore, Smith claimed that
Nebuchadnezzar's eagle feathers and bird claws were "as every mans haire and nailes will
do, if he do not pare them" (Sermons, M7 r ). Smith insisted that the Babylonian king "was
not changed in bodie, but in mind: not in shape, but in qualitie" (Sermons, M7 r ). This, in
turn, reinforced Nebuchadnezzar's exemplary function, as Smith urged his congregation:
"if you have not considered the beastlines of sin, looke upon Nebuchadnezzar like a
beast" (Sermons, M7 r ). As in the Geneva translation, Smith used simile to underscore
the figurative possibilities of "beastlines" as a reference to sin. This was essential to his
exemplary function, bridging the gap between the image of Nebuchadnezzar residing
with beasts and the moral lesson of his punishment.
This exemplary reading of Nebuchadnezzar's punishment developed out of Calvin's
refashioning of the Babylonian king in light of Protestant penitential doctrine. The
reformer had itemized the stages of repentance in his work of systematic theology,
The Institutes of Christian Religion, first published in Latin in 1536, and revised and
expanded in 1559 -the same year as he began his lectures on Daniel. 43 In The Institutes,
Calvin had underscored that the work of repentance was internal, cautioning against
outward penitential displays without due inward process. 44 Discussing the "fruits of
repentance," Calvin noted that "nothing is achieved unless we begin from the inner
feeling of the heart." 45 Calvin then wove this process of repentance into his lectures
on Nebuchadnezzar's narrative. This was significant because the king's outward
display of sorrow at sin risked appearing troublingly close to the Catholic sacrament
of penance. By the sixteenth century, the association between Nebuchadnezzar and
penance focused upon the translation of verse 4:24, where Daniel urges the king to
"breake of thy sinnes by righteousnes, and thine iniquities by mercie toward the
text.note: 42 The original Latin and the English translation both use the word "metamorphosis." See Calvin, Praelectiones, sig. I6 r .

poore" (Dan. 4:24). Catholic commentators argued that this verse pertained to charity as
satisfaction for sin. The Douai-Rheims translation would note that "the Prophet propo-
seth the soveraigne remedie of almes deeds, that by works of mercie, he procure Gods
mercie." 46 Calvin used this verse in his Institutes to rebut Catholic arguments that righ-
teous acts offer satisfaction for sin. 47 In his lectures on Daniel, Calvin developed his inter-
pretation of this verse and insisted that outward displays were not integral to repentance,
but rather served an exemplary function. Commenting on verse 4:24, Calvin used Neb-
uchadnezzar as an opportunity to define the process of true repentance:
If thou do aske what is repentance: it is the turnyng agayne of man unto God, from whom he
was departed. And is this conversion and returnyng onely in the handes, and the feete, and
the tounge? Nay, it rather begynneth in the hart, and then it goeth forth into outward
workes. True repentaunce then beginneth in the minde of man: to wit, that he which
would be wise in his owne conceit, should now renounce his owne wisedome and forsake
the foolishe confidence in his own wyt, and then that he should subdue his wicked and
corrupt affections and submit them unto God: then shall folow the reformation of the life
outwardly (Commentaries, R2 v ).
Here, Calvin showed the ways in which Nebuchadnezzar's penitence operated inwardly,
and "begynneth in the hart," before moving outward into the work of the hands, feet, or
tongue. This sequence of body parts operates at the boundaries of religious metaphor. It
reinforces Calvin's argument that Nebuchadnezzar did not undergo a physical transfor-
mation, illuminating his human corporeality. Yet the sequence of "the handes, the feete,
and the tongue" also alludes to the actions, movements, and words that each part offers as
an outward sign of repentance. Therefore, when Nebuchadnezzar praises God at the end
of Daniel 4, Calvin insisted "that which he speaketh must needes come forth of the
inward and lively feeling of the hart." Nebuchadnezzar's speech was "the fruite of his
repentaunce" (Commentaries, S4 r , T3 v ). This public confession was borne of his internal
repentance. In this respect, his speech is an outward signifier of an inward process that
offers a model for others to follow. Writing on repentance in Protestant England, Alec
Ryrie has put it succinctly that "[t]rue repentance is what you feel." 48 Although this
appeals to a sense of Protestant interiority, it does not quite capture Calvin's reading
of Nebuchadnezzar. Rather, the Babylonian king underscored that true repentance
begins with what you feel, before dictating what you do. This enabled Nebuchadnezzar
to act as an example to others.
Smith developed Calvin's sense of Nebuchadnezzar's exemplary penitence further still.
He followed Calvin that repentance took place in the heart, noting: "Nebuchaznezzar
shewes that he had understanding, and was like a man; because he gave praise to God,
and was moved in heart to worship him which made him" (Sermons, N3 v ). Being
"moved" in the heart ultimately elicits praise and worship from a sinful king. Smith
underscored this idea through a series of allusions to the body: "when the heart is
once lift up, it will lift up the eyes, and the hand, and voyce, and all, to heaven"
(Sermons, N1 r ). This sequence of images operates between the physical body and

process. As a result, Nebuchadnezzar becomes an exemplary penitent, and Smith
exhorted his congregation that "every man should trie his wisedome: for so soone as
understanding commeth to him, as it came to Nebuchadnezzar, it will extort praier
and obedience from him" (Sermons, N3 v ). Despite its grass-eating beast-cohabiting
strangeness, Nebuchadnezzar's narrative became a template of repentance for "every
man" to follow.
Exemplarity in motion
Smith's early reception is testament to his capacity to use biblical narrative as an example
of reformed doctrine. Smith spent the last years before his death in 1591 preparing his
sermons for the press. His collected sermons were published a year later. 49 This made
for a popular product almost immediately, elevating him to become "Elizabethan Eng-
land's best-selling preacher." 50 The collection went through four editions before the
end of the sixteenth century -and over twenty-one by 1675. 51 In the preface to his col-
lected sermons, Smith gave his readers instructions for the best ways to engage with his
work in print: "Read, pray, and meditate: thy profit shall be little in any booke, unlesse
thou read alone, and unles thou reade all, and record after, as the Bereans did the
Sermons of Paul" (Sermons, A3 v ). 52 Smith provides an image of the solitary and attentive
reader, yet one who is part of an imagined congregation, in the analogy to Paul and the
Bereans. A copy of the 1593 imprint of Smith's sermons demonstrates that readers took
his instructions seriously. The title page bears the signature of Esdras Coxall -perhaps
the seventeenth-century Sussex clergyman. 53 Throughout the collection, a hand has
underlined particular passages of interest, and made marginal annotations extracting
maxims. Therefore, when Smith's Pride of Nabuchadnezzar sermon reads "Humilitie
(saith Solomon) goeth before honour," the annotator has removed the homiletic and bib-
lical context, opting simply for "Humilitie goeth before honour" in the margin. 54 The
annotations continue largely in this vein throughout the Nebuchadnezzar sermons,
with marginal insertions such as "Vengeance stayeth til sinne groweth ripe" or, "God
pulleth down the proud and giveth grace to the humble." 55 However, when Smith's
text discussed Nebuchadnezzar's transformation, the marginal annotations took partic-
ular interest in the biblical narrative, adding: "Nabuchadnezzar changed not in bodie,

process. Like Calvin and Smith, the note reduces the supernatural quality of Nebuchad-
nezzar's story in order to extract religious meaning from his example.
Beyond this annotated copy of Smith's collected sermons, there is a notebook in the
British Library that attests to his attentive readership. The book in question, Harley
MS 6534, is a quarto-sized manuscript volume, and contains notes on printed
sermons, as well as general commonplace maxims. Under the heading "Notes of Certaine
Sermons of Master Henry Smith," the annotator progressed sequentially through Smith's
collected sermons including the Nebuchadnezzar trilogy. Given that this note-taker used
the margins to track the page numbers of the edition that they were using, it is possible to
say with some certainty that they were making notes from one of the editions published
by Thomas Man (or his sons) between 1604 and 1631. Although the manuscript was
written in at least three hands, a single hand composed the notes on Smith. It is likely
that these notes were made in around 1633 -including on Smith's Nebuchadnezzar
sermons. 57 Reading distantly, it might be wise to hesitate before drawing conclusions
from this volume alone, for the note-taker appears to have extracted most frequently
from the top and bottom of the page, with a mid-page lull in attention. 58 However,
reading more closely, this book provides insight into Nebuchadnezzar's exemplarity.
The notes attend to moments in the sermons that illustrated the king's moral and pen-
itent exemplarity, and removed them from their homiletic and biblical context. For
instance, Smith's Fall sermon insisted that "Daniel shewes what reckoning God keepes
of our monthes, weekes, and daies, which he gives us to repent, as he did Nebuchadnez-
zar" (Sermons, M3 r ). 59 When the note-taker came to this line, they struck through both
Daniel and Nebuchadnezzar. On the page, this leaves only the core of the sentence:
"Reckoning God keeps of our months, & weekes, and days which he gives us to
repent." 60 The notebook turned Smith's reading of Daniel 4 into a universalized apho-
rism about God's watchful eye over the passage of time. This note-taker performs a
typical maneuver in repurposing a context-specific assertion into a much more general-
ized and applicable idea. In extracting from the sermon, the annotator enacts a process
described by Arnold Hunt as a "cut-and-paste approach" to reading printed sermons. 61
The annotator shows the ways in which exemplary actions could be detached not only
from the narratives in which they were performed, but also from the characters who per-
formed them. In this case, Nebuchadnezzar's exemplary penitence was detached from the
character of the Babylonian king.
In this respect, this note-taker also enacts the processes of exemplarity. The manu-
script recalls an example discussed above: "Babylon all Hystoryes accord that it was
built by Semiramis before Nebuchadnezzer was borne." 62 Here, it is possible to trace

this particular moment of extra-biblical extrapolation: first stated by Diodorus, amplified
across Europe by Calvin, projected into England by Smith and ultimately residing in a
manuscript notebook. In its annotated form, though, the statement does not only serve
as an indictment of Nebuchadnezzar's pride, but also as a useful, quotable chunk of histor-
ical information. The note furnishes the king's exemplarity with a touch of historical detail.
Then, the notebook also insists that Nebuchadnezzar did not undergo a physical transfor-
mation: "Consider the beastliness of sinne, looke upon Nebuchadnezzar like a beast." 63
Even in this context, the reader needed to reduce the remoteness of the narrative in
order to extract religious meaning from the sermons. By transcribing the simile here,
the note-taker reinforced the idea that sin is the subject of beastliness, not Nebuchadnez-
zar's body. Then the note-taker refitted Smith's lines on the process of penitence: "When
the heart is once lift up, it will lift up the eyes, and the hand, and voice, and all to heaven." 64
Although the synecdochic lines are quoted nearly word-for-word, they read as a maxim for
Calvin's approach to the interiority of repentance when removed from their homiletic
context. Interior processes lay the foundation for external testimonies of repentance. Con-
sequently, this notebook reveals the power of the exemplar to carry doctrinal significance,
ready to pass on to a listener or reader. It also attests to the extent that Smith stretched
Nebuchadnezzar in his sermons to bridge the gap between his singular punishment and
universal doctrine. By tracing Nebuchadnezzar through Calvin, Smith, and this notebook,
it is possible to see exemplarity in motion, as a doctrine influenced a sermon that resulted
in a commonplace maxim. In this way, the exemplar allowed reformed doctrine to be
absorbed into a more generalized truth. And yet, the notebook is also testament to the dis-
tinction between an example and its lesson, severing one from the other in search of short,
extractable statements. By reading Smith in this way, this attentive note-taker exposed the
very distance that the preacher sought to bridge.
Writing Nebuchadnezzar
By the end of the sixteenth century, exemplary readings of Nebuchadnezzar's narrative
were increasingly subject to satire and scrutiny. Nebuchadnezzar was diagnosed with a
possible case of wolf-madness by Robert Burton, dramatized in a now-lost play, and alle-
gorized by Edmund Spenser as "that great proud king of Babylon" who, on account of his
idolatrous pride, was "thrown out of dore, / Into an Oxe he was transformd of yore." 65
John Donne, in an early epigram, used Nebuchadnezzar as the basis for an anti-Spanish
quip, mocking its subject who dines "Like Nebuchadnezzar, perchance, with grass and
flowers, / A salad worse than Spanish dieting." 66 Donne focuses on the spectacle of the

edn. (Abingdon: Routledge, 2013), 1.5.47.1-5, (page 80). See too Dolven, Scenes of Instruction, 144-7.

66 John Donne, "The Liar," in The Complete Poems of John Donne, ed. Robin Robbins, rev. edn. (London: Routledge, 2010), ll.
3-4 (page 19).
J. WISEMAN
text.body:
king eating grass, and refits his moral function to mock simultaneously its subject and
Spanish culinary culture. A similar comic negotiation with Nebuchadnezzar's narrative
occurs in Shakespeare's All's Well That Ends Well, where the fool Lavatch jests that
"I am no great Nebuchadnezzar, sir; I have not much skill in grass." 67 The joke ironizes
Nebuchadnezzar's narrative arc by punning that his punishment furnished him botanical
expertise as well as redemptive grace -especially given that the word "grass" would have
sounded as a near-homophone of the word "grace." 68 The fool uses the king as an exem-
plar, but learns the wrong lesson when Nebuchadnezzar's image of punishment and sal-
vation finds its comic reference in salad leaves. In this line, Lavatch capitalizes upon the
distance between the exemplary subject and its moral lesson. The joke alludes to the vivid
strangeness of a fallen king eating grass with eagle feathers and bird-like claws. This
image cannot operate as an example of grace without the intrusion of grass. The universal
moral lesson cannot be severed entirely from the particular image of a feathery, taloned,
grass-eating king. In King Lear, a comparable narrative arc of a mad king's fall turns
tragic as exemplary rhetoric fails to instill moral lessons. 69
Moving through forms and genres, Nebuchadnezzar could operate as a cautionary tale
urging his audience away from pride, and as a model of repentance professing reformed
doctrine. For Calvin, Nebuchadnezzar was capable of criticizing overreaching monar-
chies while also displaying exemplary reformed penitence. Smith used this material to
bring Nebuchadnezzar into the streets of Elizabethan London, ultimately urging his con-
gregation to imitate the Babylonian king's introspection and not leave their "understand-
ing at the Tavernes" (Sermons, N2 v ). Timothy Hampton has commented that, in
Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, "the presentation of models from the past is accompanied
by a sharp awareness that all heroes are first and foremost representations." 70 Smith's
sermons gloss over this type of representational awareness in service of a homiletic
and rhetorical framework that privileged exhortation. Yet this also required the preacher
to bridge the distance between Nebuchadnezzar's narrative and its moral lessons of sin
and salvation. In this case, exemplarity serves both a doctrinal and rhetorical function,

drawing together the narrative's singularity and its universal relevance as an example of
repentance. Between Calvin and Smith, the Babylonian king was not only a mad tyrant
but also an exemplary penitent who, with the right rhetorical application, could speak
urgently to the lives of English churchgoers and readers alike. In this respect, Nebuchad-
nezzar's fall acts as something of an exemplary exemplar. It demonstrates the capacity of
humanist rhetoric to absorb post-Reformation doctrine even when applied to the most
remote and arcane narrative material.
